blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Relate PED to total spending on a product and to the seller's revenue: multiply price by quantity, see how the total moves when price rises or falls under elastic, inelastic and unit-elastic demand, and keep revenue and profit apart.
blocks.repair_note: coverage gaps filled from syllabus guidance

blocks.heading: Spending, revenue, and the two rules
blocks.text: Total spending by consumers on a good equals the price multiplied by the quantity sold - the seller's revenue from the good. Elasticity decides which way the total moves when price moves. Where demand is price-inelastic, a price rise tends to raise total spending, because quantity demanded falls by a smaller percentage than the price rose, so the bigger price wins. Where demand is price-elastic, the same rise tends to lower it, because quantity demanded falls by a larger percentage, so the lost customers win. A price cut runs the rules in mirror.

blocks.heading: One price rise, two totals
blocks.text: The inelastic case from section 2.7.2: the Ruacana minibus at N$40 carrying 500 passengers earned spending of N$20 000 a month, since 40 x 500 = 20000. At N$60 with 460 passengers, spending is N$27 600, since 60 x 460 = 27600 - up N$7 600, because the 8 per cent fall in passengers was smaller than the 50 per cent rise. The elastic case: Kaoko Juice at N$10 sold 200 bottles, spending N$2 000, since 10 x 200 = 2000; at N$12 with 150 bottles it is N$1 800, since 12 x 150 = 1800, a fall of N$200. On the diagram, each total is the rectangle from the origin to that point on the curve, height the price and base the quantity: elasticity decides which rectangle is larger.

blocks.heading: Price cuts, and the unit-elastic case
blocks.text:
A price cut runs the two rules in mirror. Where demand is price-elastic, a cut tends to raise total spending, because quantity demanded rises by a larger percentage than the price fell. Where demand is price-inelastic, a cut tends to lower total spending, because quantity demanded rises by a smaller percentage than the price fell, so the lower price on every unit outweighs the few extra units sold.

Worked case, inelastic: a bakery in Ondangwa cuts its loaf from N$14 to N$12 and sales rise from 1 000 to 1 050 loaves a week. The price fell by 2 / 14 x 100 = 14.3 per cent; quantity rose by 50 / 1 000 x 100 = 5 per cent; PED = 5 / 14.3 = 0.35, so demand is inelastic. Spending falls from N$14 x 1 000 = N$14 000 to N$12 x 1 050 = N$12 600, a loss of N$1 400 a week. Worked case, elastic: a guesthouse in Keetmanshoop cuts its room rate from N$600 to N$540 a night, 10 per cent, and bookings rise from 100 to 130 nights a month, 30 per cent; PED = 30 / 10 = 3. Spending rises from N$60 000 to N$540 x 130 = N$70 200, a gain of N$10 200.

Unit elasticity sits between the two. Where PED is exactly 1, the change in quantity offsets the change in price, so total spending is unchanged whichever way the price moves; on the diagram, the rectangle under the old point and the rectangle under the new point have the same area. A seller facing unit-elastic demand gains no revenue from changing its price, a seller facing inelastic demand tends to gain from a rise and lose from a cut, and a seller facing elastic demand tends to do the opposite.

blocks.heading: Revenue is not profit, and one market is not the whole economy
blocks.text: Two confusions travel here. Revenue against profit: revenue is the money coming in from sales, profit what remains after the costs of production are paid, so a revenue rise settles nothing about profit until costs are known. One product against total demand: this elasticity is the responsiveness of buyers of one good, one market at a time. A total is not an average: total spending is price times quantity, an average divides a total by a count. The test for each: name what the figure adds up, and over what.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: The totals reuse section 2.7.2's calculations and are what a firm's price decision (2.7.5) and a government's tax decision (topic 4.3) turn on.
